In every game: tap Hint for the phone to suggest a move, and Undo to take one back. When a move is refused, the reason appears at the bottom.

Players take turns marking a square. You win by lining up three marks across, down or diagonally. A full board with no line is a draw.\n\nPlayed correctly by both sides, tic-tac-toe always draws — which is why the phone never loses on hard.

Brazilian draughts, on an 8 by 8 board, on the dark squares.

A man moves one square diagonally forwards, but captures both forwards AND backwards. A king moves any distance diagonally.

Capturing is compulsory, and you must capture the maximum: if one move takes three pieces and another takes one, only the three counts. Jumping several pieces is a single move — tap the square where the piece ends up.

A man reaching the last rank becomes a king. If it only passes through the last rank mid-capture, it does not.

Twenty moves with no capture and no man moving forwards is a draw.

The board starts with two discs of each colour in the middle. Black moves first.

You may only play where the new disc traps a line of your opponent's discs between it and another disc of yours — across, down or diagonally. Every trapped disc flips colour.

A player with no legal move passes automatically. The game ends when neither can play, and whoever has more discs wins.

Corners matter: a disc in a corner can never be trapped again.

Full chess. White moves first.

A pawn moves one square forwards, or two on its first move, and captures diagonally. Reaching the last rank it becomes any piece you choose — the app asks which.

The rules that are usually missing are all here: castling (with all three conditions), en passant capture, stalemate, the fifty-move rule, insufficient material, and the threefold repetition draw.

Your king may never be left in check at the end of your move. No legal move with the king in check is checkmate; no legal move without check is stalemate, which is a draw.

Block dominoes with the full set of 28, for two to four players. Each player gets seven and the rest go to the boneyard — with four players the tiles run out on the deal and there is no boneyard.

Whoever holds the highest double opens; if neither has one, the highest tile opens.

On your turn, tap a tile in your hand to lay it against one end of the line. If it fits both ends, the app asks which. With nothing that fits you draw from the boneyard automatically until you can play; with the boneyard empty you pass.

You win by playing your last tile. If the table goes all the way round on passes alone the game is blocked, and whoever holds fewer pips wins.

Your opponent's hand stays hidden — from the phone too: all you see is how many tiles they hold.

Brazilian canastra, two or three players (solo) or four (in partnerships: the player across from you is your partner). Two decks, four jokers and thirteen cards each.

A turn has three beats: draw (from the stock or the whole discard pile), meld whatever you like, and discard. The discard is what ends your turn.

THE NORMAL MELD is a RUN of three or more cards in a row of the same suit (four to ace — the two is always a wildcard and the three never enters), with at most one wildcard filling a gap or an end. A SET (three or more cards of the same rank) also exists, but may only be melded after the partnership already has a canasta.

With the exact card in hand, you can swap the wildcard out of a run already on the table: it does not go back to your hand, it slides to a free end of that same meld, which grows by one card.

Seven cards make a CANASTA: clean is worth 200, dirty is worth 100 — and what makes it dirty is the TWO, not the joker. In a CLEAN canasta, every card past the seventh is worth another 100.

VALUES: joker and two are worth 50; three is worth 100; eight through king are worth 10; ace is worth 20; four through seven are worth 5.

RED THREE: never played. It is worth 100 points sitting on the table — only if the partnership has a canasta — and goes there by itself as soon as it appears; draw one from the stock and you take another card in its place.

BLACK THREE AND WILDCARDS: both block the pile when discarded, stopping the next player from taking the discard pile. A black three never melds — holding it costs 100 points in hand.

DEAD HAND: only one, and only with two or three players — partnerships play without it. It belongs to whoever runs out of cards first, and taking it is not going out: you pick up the thirteen cards and the hand carries on.

GOING OUT means running out of cards when there is no dead hand left to take, and that requires a canasta. Every time the partnership runs out of cards — taking the dead hand or going out for real — it scores 50, and both can happen in the same hand.

At the end of the hand, what is on the table adds up and what is left in hand subtracts. The match runs to 3000.

Hearts, four players, full 52-card deck. Winning tricks is bad here: every heart is worth 1 point and the queen of spades is worth 13. The match ends when somebody reaches 100, and whoever has the FEWEST points wins.

Before each hand everyone passes three cards: to the left, to the right, across, and then a fourth hand with no passing — after which the rotation starts over.

Whoever holds the 2 of clubs leads, and leads with it. You must follow the suit that was led; without it, anything goes. No penalty cards on the first trick.

Hearts may only be led once they have already appeared in a trick — or when they are all you have left.

The highest card of the suit led takes the trick, along with any points on the table.

Shooting the moon: take all 26 points in a hand and you score none, while the other three score 26 each.

Pife for two to four players. Two decks with one joker each, nine cards apiece, the rest becomes the stock and one card opens the discard pile.

A turn has two beats: draw a card (from the stock or the top of the discard pile) and throw one away. The discard is what ends your turn.

You win by holding nine cards that close into three groups of three. A group is either three of the same rank or three in sequence in the same suit. A joker fits into either one, filling the gap — but a group of nothing but jokers does not count.

The ace is high, and only high: Q-K-A closes a run, A-2-3 does not.

The check happens after the discard, on the nine cards left: with ten in hand, closing three groups and having one over is the same thing as throwing that one away.

What your opponent discards is information: the top of the pile is face up, and they can take yours too. When the stock runs out the discard pile is shuffled back in, minus the top card. If nobody closes after the deck has gone round three times, the hand is a draw.

Solitaire (Klondike), for one player. Twenty-eight cards in seven columns — one in the first, seven in the last —, the rest in the stock, and four foundations to fill.

The goal is to move all 52 cards to the foundations, one per suit, from ace to king.

In the columns cards run down: each one goes onto a card one rank higher and of the opposite colour. Here the ace is the lowest card of all — the king closes a column at the top and the ace at the bottom.

An empty column only takes a king. Tapping a card in the middle of a column picks it up along with everything above it: the run travels together.

A face-down card that becomes exposed turns itself over. That is the game: turning cards over is the only thing that really opens it up.

You draw one card at a time, and the pile goes back to the stock as many times as you need, always in the same order.

A card can come back down from a foundation — sometimes it is the only way to unstick the table.

You cannot lose. Either all 52 go up, or a moment comes when nothing else can move, and the app says so instead of leaving you hunting for a move that is not there.

Truco mineiro, for two or four players (in partnerships: the player across from you is your partner). A 40-card deck — the 8, 9 and 10 come out —, three cards each, and the match runs to 12 points.

CARD ORDER, weakest to strongest: 4, 5, 6, 7, Q, J, K, A, 2, 3.

MANILHAS: four cards beat every other card, and in truco mineiro they are FIXED — no turned-up card decides anything. Strongest to weakest: 4♣ (zap), 7♥ (copas), A♠ (espadilha), 7♦ (ourito). Note that the zap is a four: the other three fours are still the weakest card in the deck. A manilha is the card, not the rank.

The hand is decided in the best of three rounds. The strongest card played wins the round.

TIES: a tied round is not replayed — it stays tied, and the tiebreak comes from whoever won the first round. Win the first and tie the second, and you take the hand. Tie the first, and you must win the second. Tie the third, and the first round decides again. And a hand with all three rounds tied belongs to nobody: no one scores.

THE CALL: the hand starts worth 1. On your turn, before playing a card, you may call truco and propose 3. The other side accepts, runs, or asks for more — 6, 9, 12. Whoever runs hands the opponent what the hand was worth BEFORE the call: running from a truco costs 1, from a six costs 3, from a nine costs 6.

Asking for more accepts the previous value along the way — that is why running from a six already costs three.

Whoever called and was accepted passes the word along: only the other side may raise next.

Ludo for two to four players, four tokens each. On a table of two the colours start from opposite corners.

The app rolls the die, not you: when your turn comes the value is already on screen, and the choice is which token moves.

Only a 6 brings a token out of the yard. Rolling a 6 also earns another turn.

Landing on an opponent token sends it back to the yard — except on the marked squares, which are safe.

Coming home is exact: two squares short, a 5 is no good and the token stays put. You win by bringing all four tokens home.
